```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The 90-day goal is a paying customer, and only B shows evidence that end users pay. Five live, sourced competitors charge real prices: SplitKin $4.99/mo, CircleCare $6.99/mo, CompassCare $3.99/mo, Caring Village $14.99–$24.99/mo and TendTo $11.99–$19.99/mo. A solo operator inherits a proven price anchor.",
    "A's own brief says there is no clean single payer. Every named direct competitor is free to the end user and funded by grants, VC or nonprofit dues. The closest paid analog, Pointz, needed $520k in outside funding and does not publish its subscription price.",
    "B names a clear payer: the primary adult-child caregiver, with siblings joining free. A's payer options (municipalities, advocacy nonprofits, insurers) are listed as open questions, and those would mean long B2B or public-sector sales cycles that are hard to close within 90 days.",
    "B's demand evidence is unprompted, recurring pain from caregivers on Reddit who now use spreadsheets and group texts. A's demand evidence is a one-line HN wish, nonprofit marketing copy and a competitor founder's origin story. None of these shows intent to pay.",
    "A also has a cold-start problem that B lacks. A crowdsourced hazard map is worthless without data density in a city, while a care-coordination tool gives value to a single family on day one.",
    "B's risks are real but are mainly about scale, not about landing a first paying customer. They include six or more competitors, users who say they want it free, short customer lifetime and multi-sibling activation friction. Proven existing price points make one paying customer in 90 days much more plausible than in A."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's 'Case For' calls a 'credible non-consumer payer path (municipal Vision Zero programs, research grants)' a strength, but it is unsourced. No municipality or Vision Zero program is cited as having paid a third-party vendor for this kind of tool. The only funding evidence is BikeMaps.org's $930k government research grant, which went to an academic project, not a solo vendor. The brief's own Open Question #1 admits it is unknown whether cities would pay at all. Under the rules this claim counts as missing, which leaves A with no evidenced payer.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-high confidence. The key separator is direct evidence of consumer willingness to pay, which B has and A lacks. B's own evidence cuts against it in places: one Reddit quote says caregivers want it free, several competitors offer generous free tiers, and channel CAC is unproven. B could still struggle to differentiate or scale, but for a first paying customer within 90 days, it is the clearly better bet."
}
```
